what_its_for: Ceftaroline fosamil is an antibiotic used to treat two types of infections: (1) skin and skin structure infections, including those caused by MRSA (a hard-to-treat type of staph bacteria), and (2) community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (a lung infection you can get outside of a hospital). It works by stopping bacteria from building their protective outer wall, which kills them.
how_to_take: This medicine is given through an IV (intravenous) line directly into your vein, usually in a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. A healthcare professional will prepare and give you each dose. The infusion typically takes about 60 minutes. You will NOT inject this yourself at home unless specifically trained and instructed by your healthcare team. Each dose comes as a powder that is mixed with liquid before it is given to you.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 600 mg given every 12 hours (twice a day) for 5 to 14 days, depending on your type of infection. Your doctor may adjust your dose if you have kidney problems. Children's doses are based on age and weight and will be determined by your doctor. Always follow the exact schedule your doctor or nurse gives you.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare professional in a clinical setting, it is very important that you keep all of your scheduled infusion appointments. If you miss an appointment, call your doctor or infusion center right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not try to double up doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: You do not need to store this medication at home in most cases, as it is prepared and stored by healthcare professionals. If you have been given pre-mixed infusion bags for home use, store them in the refrigerator (36°F to 46°F or 2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze them. Once mixed, the solution must be used within the time your pharmacist specifies. Keep out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medications, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting this medicine. Avoid skipping doses or stopping treatment early, even if you feel better — finishing the full course of treatment helps prevent the infection from coming back and reduces the risk of antibiotic resistance. Let your healthcare team know if you have a known allergy to penicillin or other cephalosporin antibiotics, as you may be at higher risk for an allergic reaction.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: a rash, hives, or itching; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing (signs of a serious allergic reaction); severe diarrhea or stomach cramps that may be watery or bloody (could be a serious gut infection called C. diff); yellowing of your skin or eyes; unusual bruising or bleeding; seizures; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also call your doctor if your infection does not seem to be improving after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: Many patients start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting treatment. However, it is very important to complete the entire prescribed course of treatment even if you feel better sooner. Stopping too early can allow the bacteria to come back and become harder to treat. Your doctor will monitor your progress and decide when it is safe to stop treatment.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Your dose may be lowered if your kidneys are not working well. Your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of this drug during pregnancy is not fully established, so your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks. Elderly patients (65 and older): Older adults may need a dose adjustment if they have reduced kidney function, which is common with aging. Children: This drug can be used in children, including newborns, but the dose will be carefully calculated by the doctor based on the child's weight and age.
